summary: We are testing whether reducing the branch-and-bound (B&B) solver's ternary search iterations from 20→12 and adding an 800ms time guard eliminates intermittent score drops (85-95 range) caused by Docker timing variability, while maintaining the perfect score of 100. An ablation arm removes B&B entirely to quantify its contribution over greedy+local-search alone.
key_points: H-main: Optimized B&B (12 ternary iterations + 800ms clock() time guard). Predicted score: 100. The ternary precision at 12 iterations (~2e-6) is still far tighter than needed for integer LP bounds, giving ~40% fewer bound evaluations per node. The time guard ensures that if B&B runs too long in Docker, we gracefully fall back to the greedy+LS result.

H-ablation: B&B removed, keeping only 23-variant greedy heuristics + local search. Predicted score: ~85. This isolates B&B's contribution — iter-1 data showed 11/20 test cases are suboptimal without B&B.

Confirmation criteria: H-main scores 100 (or very close) → time guard + reduced iterations solves the reliability problem. H-ablation scores significantly below 100 (expected ~85) → B&B is necessary. If H-main still drops below 95, we'd diagnose whether the time guard triggered (Docker is slower than expected) or whether 12 ternary iterations loosened bounds enough to blow up the B&B tree.

Risk check: The design is well-scoped — only 2 arms, each requiring a single judge call (~45s). The code changes are minimal (change a constant, add 3 lines for time guard; comment out 2 lines for ablation). No new algorithmic mechanisms are introduced.

Context from iter-1: The full B&B solver scored 100 in most runs but occasionally dropped to 85-95, likely due to Docker timing variability causing TLE on some test cases. Greedy-only (no B&B, no local search) scored 0 because it couldn't beat the NSA baseline.
